title: All the Songs in Disney’s ‘Hexed,’ Including a New Cover From Hailee Steinfeld
summary: It's witchy and magical, as you'd hope The post All the Songs in Disney’s ‘Hexed,’ Including a New Cover From Hailee Steinfeld appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Disney’s “Hexed” is the studio’s Thanksgiving offering this year, and it’s got a pretty magical soundtrack to go with the witchiness of the film. The animated feature stars Hailee Steinfeld as Billie Doe, a young witch who only learns she’s a witch as a teenager. But that’s only because her mom, Alice (Rashida Jones), purposefully suppressed and hid Billie’s powers in order to keep her safe. Obviously, Billie isn’t going to really understand that right away, and what follows is a story of mothers and daughters, and how they come to understand each other. Despite having Steinfeld as the lead, and being a Disney animated film , it’s not actually a musical. But that’s not to say that Steinfeld doesn’t sing at all. Here are all the songs in Disney’s “Hexed.” “My Girl” by The Mamas & The Papas “I Want to Break Free” by Queen “Levitating” by Dua Lipa “Yo Ho (A Pirate’s Life for Me)” “Black Magic” by Little Mix “Confident” by Demi Lovato “Magic” by Hailee Steinfeld Disney’s “Hexed” is now in theaters everywhere. title: ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Reveals the Bloody Scene He Cut for Film’s PG-13 Rating
summary: Francis Lawrence says every "Hunger Games" movie he's helmed automatically gets an R rating from the MPA The post ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Reveals the Bloody Scene He Cut for Film’s PG-13 Rating appeared first on TheWrap .
content: This story contains spoilers from “Sunrise on the Reaping.” “The Hunger Games” film franchise is filled with violence — the whole premise of the titular Games is that there’s only one survivor — but “Sunrise on the Reaping” director Francis Lawrence says he scaled back the blood in the latest film. Speaking on the “On Film … With Kevin McCarthy” podcast released Monday, Lawrence, who has directed every single “Hunger Games” since the first film, explained his regular debate with the Motion Picture Association (MPA) and their rating system. “Every Hunger Games movie we turn in automatically gets an R and we start a back and forth,” Lawrence explained. “I’ve even found on this latest HG film that the tastes feel a little more conservative,” the director said of the organization that determines rating. “They’re a little more sensitive than they were three years ago on ‘Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes.'” “Sunrise on the Reaping” is rated PG-13 for “strong violence, bloody images, disturbing material, some smoking and teen drinking.” Lawrence said he had to tweak the prequel that focuses on Haymitch Abernathy four or five times to reach the PG-13 rating. He then explained which scenes were scaled back or trimmed. “One of the last things that we went back and forth on is the axe throw with Silka,” Lawrence said. “When Silka throws her axe and then it breaks apart and the axe head goes into her chest. It took longer for her to die. There was more shots of her there with the axe buried into her chest and her kind of gasping for breath.” The director admitted the one scene he really wanted to keep was around the death of Mckenna Grace’s character Maysilee. “We had a very specific neck wound on Maysilee in her death where basically the one that kills her is right here,” he said, pointing to his throat. “And [Haymitch is] covering it and when his hand comes off you can see blood starting to drip out of it and you could see the hole and it’s why she can’t speak.” “And they made us get rid of that and that was the one that killed me,” Lawrence admitted. However, he says he was mindful of writer Suzanne Collins’ intended audience and didn’t want the violence to be gratuitous. “In the end, [the Hunger Games films] are anti-violence stories,” Lawrence explained. “They’re about the consequence of war, the consequence of violence.” “The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping” is currently in theaters. The post ‘Sunrise on the Reaping’ Director Reveals the Bloody Scene He Cut for Film’s PG-13 Rating appeared first on TheWrap .

title: ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Review: Netflix Hit Becomes Its Own Worst Enemy
summary: Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman’s game performances can’t save this pulpy sexcapade from itself The post ‘The Hunting Wives’ Season 2 Review: Netflix Hit Becomes Its Own Worst Enemy appeared first on TheWrap .
content: The phrase “body count” can mean vastly different things depending on the audience. To some, it’s the accumulation of a killer’s unfortunate victims. To those raised on TikTok, it means a person’s collective sexual conquests. To “The Hunting Wives,” it’s all the above. Netflix’s surprise hit series about living large and behaving badly in Texas is back for Season 2 and if there was ever a question of whether creator Rebecca Cutter might pull back the reins on this increasingly chaotic story, audiences will learn quickly they’ve apparently removed the word “restraint” from the Lone Star State’s dictionaries. Originally produced for Starz before it was licensed by Netflix, the series fronted by an admirably game Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman came out of nowhere last year and left its audience panting. Not just from the intensely sexual and unabashedly queer storylines, but also from the brisk marathon required to keep up with its plot. Brittany Snow as Sophie in “The Hunting Wives” (Credit: Netflix) Politically liberal but socially conservative Sophie (Snow) moved to Texas after her husband took a job working for Republican oil tycoon and gubernatorial wannabe Jeb Banks (Dermot Muloney). Her progressive sensibilities bristled at the overt anti-abortion, pro-gun community she was suddenly swallowed up by. But none of her so-called values — moral or otherwise — stood a chance against the allure of Jed’s wife Margo (Akerman), a queenbee socialite with a hunger for men 20 years her junior and women her own age. Over the course of eight episodes, Sophie virtually imploded her life, pushed away her dud of a husband and otherwise absent son, and willingly gave herself over to the party drug that is Margo, only to find she was yet another pawn in a larger game of murder and mayhem. It was as if “Melrose Place” was much gayer and co-sponsored by the Second Amendment. But the knowingly cheeky series based on the novel by May Cobb returns with an inflated ego from its success and money to burn as one of Netflix’s newest golden children. But it also has a lot to prove. “The Hunting Wives” got lucky. It got bought by the right streamer, it hit at the right time (the dead of summer when it had little competition), and its willingness to laugh at its own brash sensationalism was rewarded with its moment basking in the zeitgeist. But Season 2 arrives having not listened to any of the criticism about its unhinged narrative and its characters’ frustrating lack of self-awareness or self-preservation. Instead, the new episodes lean almost comically into the oncoming train of insanity. Is that what audiences want? It’s almost certainly what they liked before, and “The Hunting Wives” remains an undoubtedly fun watch if you can turn off that logic-driven part of your brain that Sophie does whenever she sees Margo. But this season, whether its two characters bringing each other to completion in the women’s bathroom of a honky tonk or a killing spree as a means of working through trauma, nothing feels truly consequential when everyone is living their lives at 125mph. This also isn’t a flash-in-the-pan show anymore. It can’t just shock audiences to stay alive. It has to justify its continued existence and their commitment to coming back. Brittany Snow and Malin Akerman in “The Hunting Wives” (Netflix) The new episodes find Sophie and Margo trying — and to no one’s shock, failing — to steer clear of each other, even while Sophie clings to the shreds of her life and dignity. Thankfully, beyond their cyclical bad decision making, other characters try out new trajectories in life, even if they are fleeting. Callie (Jaime Ray Newman), Margo’s sometimes lover and best friend, becomes the star of “Married Justice,” a “Real Housewives” knockoff for decadently conservative women with husbands in law enforcement. With the added spotlight and an unexpected new scene partner, Newman emerges as a ringer for “Hunting Wives” MVP. Elsewhere, Brad (George Ferrier), Margo’s (other) sometimes lover and the survivor of Season 1’s body count (RIP to his mother, girlfriend and mental health!), manages to move forward in college only to succumb to the demons of grief, abuse, drugs, orgies and John Stamos as a sleazy music producer. The fact that Brad’s storyline runs out of gas midway through the season is a testament to just how quickly this series is chewing through material. Also fast and furious is a new storyline with recent “Widow’s Bay” Emmy nominee Dale Dickey, who rides in as the matriarch of a biker gang hunting down Margo’s brother — you know, the one Sophie killed and dumped in a lake at the end of last season. By the time the bodies start hitting the floor, the culprits aren’t all that surprising because their hands are already soaked in blood, and far too many twists rely on the audience forgetting how recently Margo and Sophie, specifically, killed someone. All of this is sloppy narrative fodder that should burn as hot as it does fast. But the show’s rejection of nuance gives way to exhaustion by season’s end — hell, it’s exhausting just finishing an episode. If audiences want more sexual misdeeds, catty backstabbing and an unnecessary reminder some people really do have black holes where a soul should be, “The Hunting Wives” remains exactly what was promised. But Season 2’s final stretch exposes what could be the fatal — and most unexpected — flaw in its central conceit. Something Cobb likely never saw coming when building her palace to Southern debauchery. Jennifer Daley as Stacy, Joyce Glenn as Monae, Jaime Ray Newman as Callie, Malin Akerman as Margo, Alexandria DeBerry as Taylor in “The Hunting Wives” (Dana Hawley/Netflix) As an ode to star-crossed lovers in Sophie and Margo, “The Hunting Wives” rests on the immovable, unflinching threat that is conservatism in Texas. In their world, these two women can never truly be together because we’re told the power of Jed and those like him is simply too big to defeat. But “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 arrives in a new world where this simply isn’t true. This month’s midterm election proved even Texas can be felled by the unlikeliest of cultural pendulums. In the aftermath of the election, a late Season 2 discussion about the importance of an endorsement from the unnamed but Trump-coded president is almost laughable now. The real world has undercut Sophie and Margo’s defense that they are merely trying to be together in this big bad world. But if America can dismantle the system keeping these doomed lovers down, what happens when they actually have to face the question they can’t stop running from –– are we the problem in our own story? (Hint: the answer is a “hell yes” the size of Texas.) “The Hunting Wives” Season 2 is now streaming on Netflix. title: Adam Sandler Cheers Ezra Frech’s ‘DWTS’ Win With Heartfelt Video Message: ‘You’ve Always Been the Man’
summary: The "Happy Gilmore" actor has been a longtime supporter of the Frech family's Angel City Sports org The post Adam Sandler Cheers Ezra Frech’s ‘DWTS’ Win With Heartfelt Video Message: ‘You’ve Always Been the Man’ appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Adam Sandler did backflips over Ezra Frech’s “Dancing With the Stars” Season 35 win on Wednesday, sharing a heartfelt video message that congratulated the 21-year-old for taking the crown. The “Happy Gilmore” actor and 21-year-old American Paralympic track-and-field athlete and disability rights advocate first connected over the Frech family’s Angel City Sports organization in Southern California when the “DWTS” star was just a child. “Ezra — oh my goodness, you are the king again! You are just a stud,” Sandler said in the video message, posted to his personal X page. “We’ve known you since you were a little kid. You’ve always been the man. We’ve always loved you, we’ve always talked about you. You are and have been since elementary school a massive inspiration for all, and you did it again buddy. You inspired the world.” The actor then wished Frech “continued success” and shared his love. “We love you. Enjoy this moment. Love to the family, from all of us, OK buddy? Congrats!” pic.twitter.com/xfIttqgcvB — Adam Sandler (@AdamSandler) November 25, 2026 The Paralympic gold medalist and pro partner Daniella Karagach won Season 35 of “Dancing With the Stars” on Tuesday, taking home the Len Goodman Mirrorball Trophy after a three-round finale. Frech, 21, made history as the first amputee to win the ABC dance competition and the youngest man to claim the title. Thy finished ahead of figure skater Amber Glenn and Pasha Pashkov, who took second place, followed by Connor Wood and Rylee Arnold in third, Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik in fourth and Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas in fifth. The winner was determined by a combination of judges’ scores and viewer votes during the live finale, which aired across all U.S. time zones for the first time in the show’s history. title: ‘The Lowdown’ Creator Sterlin Harjo on the Season 2 Finale, That ‘No Country’ Nod and Season 3 Status
summary: The writer/director tells TheWrap about Peter Dinklage's return and why we may not have seen the last of Betty Gilpin in the FX noir comedy The post ‘The Lowdown’ Creator Sterlin Harjo on the Season 2 Finale, That ‘No Country’ Nod and Season 3 Status appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Spoilers for “The Lowdown” Season 2 finale follow below. Truth’s easy? Anything but, as Ethan Hawke’s Lee Raybon learned throughout “The Lowdown” Season 2. But just because his path was hard doesn’t mean he’s giving up, as the Season 2 finale left the excellent Tulsa-set FX noir comedy series with plenty of threads left to untangle in a potential Season 3. That was the point, creator Sterlin Harjo explained to TheWrap in an interview tied to the finale. While Lee doesn’t get the girl and doesn’t get to write his story, he learns how much he is loved, finds some solace in his relationship with his father and, of course, keeps raging against the dying light as the episode concludes with him continuing his investigation into John Hawkes’ Judge Jed. “The Lowdown” is one of the best shows on all of television, somehow growing in esteem in Season 2 with one of Tommy Lee Jones’ best performances ever (the season has a 100% on Rotten Tomatoes ). Surely that’d be enough for an automatic Season 3 greenlight, right? While Harjo said he has lots of ideas for a third season (and even knows how it opens), he cautioned that an awards boost would significantly help the show’s chances. So consider this your clarion call, voters. Do the right thing. In the meantime, read on as Harjo unpacks that Season 2 ending, explains why we may not have seen the last of Betty Gilpin’s Ginger, talks about leaning into the “No Country for Old Men” similarities with Jones’ final monologue and more. Tell me what you wanted to get across in the ending of the season, because you get to the end and Lee feels like he lost. He didn’t get the girl. He didn’t write the story he wanted. But it feels like the arc of Lee this season was far more personal than professional. What did you want to leave people with at the end? I think the irony of the season is he gets a mug that says “Truth’s Easy” and it’s anything but. I think everyone’s sort of expressing this throughout the show, even Frog to Francis. People have different truths, and I think that Lee’s idea of the truth and what he wants is challenged through the whole thing, and him having to go to these other journalists in town — that was the first thing that I thought of. Giving a speech that’s a crazy speech where you just trash everyone, and then having to, by the end, go hat in hand to them and say, “I need your help.” That was sort of the point of the season to me. But also, you have this whole thing with his father. I think that Lee has been running away from who he really is and his relationship with his father. It’s an interesting thing to make a show about someone who is obsessed with the truth but wants to hide where they come from and who they come from. That dynamic is really interesting to me. I think him coming to terms with his father and his relationship with his father helps make this decision that “Oh, the truth is way more complicated. My father was actually in Vietnam, but he’s also a liar, and I can’t do this alone, and I need help from other people.” I think all of that is just personal growth from Lee, but also extends to his professional life. I told you the last time we spoke that a lot of noir feels like karaoke but “The Lowdown” feels like the real deal, and I think you did the non-karaoke version of the father-son story here. There was no big fight in the rain or airing of grievances. That relationship played out far more subtly. I think real life is not told in these big sweeping monologues. It’s actually told through glances and asides, especially from someone like his father, and this complicated relationship they had with each other where they can’t communicate. The other side to not being able to communicate with someone is that expression is very slight and small, but it’s actually really big between them. So your father putting his hand on your back, who you hadn’t talked with in a long time, all of a sudden that’s really big. I think of it as like the love story with Dawn and Tim in the UK “Office.” Other than when he goes out on a limb and expresses his love, there weren’t these big love story moments. There were slight glances and touches on the shoulder and hugs and a kiss on the cheek, and all of a sudden these things are really big because everything else is repressed. I just think that’s good writing. With a person like Frog, you’re not going to get those moments, and you get what you can. I love the moment when he says, “It wasn’t so bad in there, in the hospital. I could have used a rest.” That’s this big cathartic apology, to the point where Lee doesn’t know what to say. It’s bigger because it’s small. I think that it’s just more truthful, and I try to approach it like that. And also Tommy Lee Jones, if you give him bullshit to say, you’re gonna hear about it. He’s probably not gonna do it, and it’ll be really obvious whenever you see it on screen. That’s kind of the benefit of writing for Tommy Lee Jones, where you’re like, well, I can’t do the cliche. I had the pressure in the last episode where he’s got this big monologue, and it’s like the fucking Coen Brothers and Cormac McCarthy obviously gave him one of the best monologues of anything at the end of “No Country for Old Men.” How do I compete with that? And I was like, well, there is no competing with them, but I can sort of give homage to it. I think that monologue is in conversation with the monologue from “No Country for Old Men.” Because it’s Tommy Lee Jones giving it, but also it is someone reflecting on life and talking about weather. So I leaned into it instead of avoiding it. Tommy Lee Jones in “The Lowdown” Season 2 finale (FX/Hulu) I think it’s one of the best performances of his entire career. It’s been really cool hearing my dad, who’s a big fan of his, going like, “Man, he is so good at this.” Hearing people that have been fans of his for a long time, it is really cool to hear that. Betty Gilpin is also incredible in the show too. I loved the postscript in Eureka Springs. Was there ever a world in which she ended up with Lee? Well there’s hopefully going to be a Season 3. I was going to ask. You’re ready to dive back in? I’m not finished with Ginger. It’s funny, I was still writing while we were making the whole thing, and so no one knew how it was going to end, and I kept getting texts from Betty, just randomly now and again, that said, “#DontKillGinger.” (Laughs) But in a similar way to the father and son story, Lee thinks that that’s what he needs, but it’s not what he needs. He’s not gonna buy blue heelers and go live in the woods and raise chickens and crush books all day because he’s got this fire inside of him to do this other thing, and that’s always going to be there. They found each other in this crisis of a time, personally. And in the real world, there is no like, “Oh, but then we walked away holding hands.” There has to be a reset, and I have ideas about what Ginger does and where she went and if she comes back. Peter Dinklage coming back was also incredible, with the Dylan Thomas monologue. How did that come together? Peter loved doing Season 1, and he’s super busy right now. So we reached out. We’re just like, “We have this. It’d be really cool to have you in this moment. If you can’t, totally cool. But if you want to make it work, let’s try.” And he was like, “Let’s do it. Let’s try.” So we flew him in for one day, and he just comes in and floors everybody. If ever there was a question of it being worth bringing Peter Dinklage in for one scene, he answers it. He was so pumped after we did it. It was such a wild funeral scene, and we were just improvising everything at a certain point. There’s this stuff that we improvised that we couldn’t put in the final episode, but it was like me and the choir and the preacher before they walk in, we’re standing there, and I always play music from a Bluetooth speaker, and I just happened to be playing “Thuggish Ruggish Bone” by Bone Thugs, and we all started dancing, and the choir and the preacher were dancing. I was like, “Holy shit, y’all should walk in like this,” and so I literally held up this Bluetooth speaker, the preacher and choir are all going down the aisle out of nowhere to “Thuggish Ruggish Bone,” it’s so funny, and then the preacher keeps quoting “Thuggish Ruggish Bone” and other things while he’s preaching. Sadly, I guess like all of Bone Thugs and Harmony are in legal disputes with each other, so you can’t use their music. So that was scrapped. It also would have been like an hour and a half episode. How are you feeling about Season 3 chances? I have ideas for Season 3, it’s up to the powers that be. I think it’d be smart for them to make Season 3. I do too! But they never let me know right off the bat. It’s a thing where like this show came out and people call it the best thing on TV, and the reviews have been amazing. Does that translate to awards? I don’t know, because I’ve never understood that. “Reservation Dogs” didn’t get nominated for a lot of awards, and I don’t think that’s because of the quality of the show, so I don’t know what sort of politics in the sky are happening when it comes to awards or whatever. But I would hope that people love the show so much that it would reflect in some of that, which would help us get a Season 3. It’s all up in the air, and I hope that we get to do it and I have ideas. I know how it’s going to open, and it’s such a wild opening that there’s a lot of great writing that has to happen with this writers’ room to make that make sense. I always sort of have a tone or scenes or an homage or something that I’m feeling for the next season, so I know a lot about what’s going to happen. But my thoughts cost money, so wait until that writers room gets ordered. I’ll just say if Tommy Lee Jones doesn’t get nominated, that’s just proof the voters didn’t watch it. Because every critic friend of mine says this is the best thing on TV right now. Put that in your article! “The Lowdown” Season 2 is now streaming in its entirety on Hulu. title: How to Watch the 2026 National Dog Show
summary: It's the goodest Thanksgiving tradition The post How to Watch the 2026 National Dog Show appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Happy Thanksgiving, folks! While you’re waiting for the turkey to be ready and your NFL game to start, what should you be watching? The National Dog Show, of course. The fanciest good boys and good girls are once again ready to compete for the title of Best in Show, as is tradition for this holiday. Last year, it was a Belgian Sheepdog named Soleil who took the title, but the 2026 champion? Well, you can only find out by watching. Here’s all the information you need. When is the National Dog Show? As always, you’ll be able to watch the National Dog Show on Thanksgiving. The broadcast airs from noon to 2 p.m. ET/PT, but the actual competition took place earlier this month. Is it streaming? Indeed it is. You can watch the broadcast live on NBC or stream the show over on Peacock. What exactly is the National Dog Show? The National Dog Show is an annual competition hosted by the Kennel Club of Philadelphia, as part of the American Kennel Club. Dogs from all over the nation compete in seven groups: herding, hound, non-sporting, sporting, terrier, toy and working. Judges are looking for the breeds who are the closest matched to the definition of what that breed is supposed to look like as defined by the American Kennel Club. What’s the prize? The honor of Best in Show is prestigious in itself, but the winner also takes home roughly $2,500 in prize money. title: How to Watch the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade
summary: The holiday isn't complete without tuning in to the annual NYC parade The post How to Watch the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade appeared first on TheWrap .
content: The Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is celebrating a major milestone, and you’ll want to tune in. The big New York City spectacle typically starts bright and early on Thanksgiving Thursday and runs for three and a half hours. The parade is full of floats, musical performances and massive balloons of your favorite characters. However, the timing has changed this year. The annual event has been postponed due to severe weather . So with a lot of last minute swapping, here is everything you need to know about how to watch the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. What time does the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade start? The annual Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade was originally supposed to start at 8:30 a.m. ET on Thursday, Nov. 26. For the first time ever, the entire event had to be pushed back due to severe weather and high winds. The parade will now air on Saturday, Nov. 28 at 8:30 a.m. ET. Where can you watch and stream the parade? The 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade is available to watch on NBC and will be streaming live on Peacock. What if I miss the parade? No worries! An encore of the full parade will play on both NBC and Peacock at 2 p.m. ET. Who is performing during the parade? With 2026 being the 100th annual parade, there are big names slated to perform. The expected performers are Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Natasha Bedingfield, Baha Men, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, Feid, EJAE, Mckenna Grace, Indigo Girls, Icona Pop, JoJo, Wyclef Jean, Queen Latifah, Il Volo, Natalie Merchant, Jamie Miller, Ryan Peter Murphy, Leslie Odom Jr., Keke Palmer, Anthony Ramos, RIIZE, Smash Mouth, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, Melissa Joan Hart, Holly Robinson Peete, Rodney Peete and Megan Hilty. There will also be a tribute to the late Dolly Parton during the performance. Various cast members from “The Book of Mormon,” “Chicago,” “Aladdin,” “Hamilton,” “The Lost Boys,” “The Rocky Horror Show,” “Schmigadoon!” and “Wicked” will also be featured in a medley of the Broadway shows. title: Bob Iger Had Extramarital Affair and Got Employee Pregnant, Tell-All Says
summary: The revelation comes from Robbie Whelan's upcoming unauthorized biography "The House of the Mouse" The post Bob Iger Had Extramarital Affair and Got Employee Pregnant, Tell-All Says appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Bob Iger had an extramarital affair and got an employee pregnant, an upcoming unauthorized biography charting the corporate history of Disney claims. The revelation is made in Robbie Whelan’s “The House of the Mouse,” which The New York Times got an advance copy of and reported on Wednesday. Whelan says the former Disney CEO had an affair with an ABC marketer in the 1990s when he was the head of ABC Entertainment, per the Times. Their relationship was consensual. (Iger divorced wife Susan Iger in 1994 and married his current wife Willow Bay in 1995.) The unnamed woman, Iger’s subordinate, became pregnant and “suffered through a traumatic termination procedure,” Whelan wrote. The author contrasted Iger’s personal behavior with his public support of the #MeToo movement in the 2010s, where powerful figures were held accountable for their inappropriate actions. Iger declined to be interviewed for the book. The 75-year-old executive served as CEO of Disney twice, first succeeding Michael Eisner in 2005 until his contract expired in 2020. He returned for his second stint in November 2022 until he was succeeded by Josh D’Amaro last March. “Josh D’Amaro is an exceptional leader and the right person to become our next CEO,” Iger said of D’Amaro’s appointment at the time. “He has an instinctive appreciation of the Disney brand, and a deep understanding of what resonates with our audiences, paired with the rigor and attention to detail required to deliver some of our most ambitious projects. His ability to combine creativity with operational excellence is exemplary and I am thrilled for Josh and the company.” “The House of Mouse: Bob Iger and the War of Succession at Disney” will be released on Dec. 1. title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Spectators Surprised by Postponement: ‘Oh No!’
summary: The annual event will take place on Saturday instead of Thursday The post Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade Spectators Surprised by Postponement: ‘Oh No!’ appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade spectators, many of whom traveled far to see the annual holiday event, expressed surprise and shock at the news that the parade has been postponed. Reporter Joelle Garguilo of ABC 7, the local news affiliate in New York City, caught up with fans who didn’t yet know the parade was moved from Thursday to Saturday. “That’s not true,” one tourist from Luxembourg said in disbelief on Wednesday. “Oh no, I’m so sad,” she added. The woman was planning to leave Friday but said she can “probably” change her travel plans to accommodate the new parade date. Two women from Hawaii gasped in disbelief when they learned of the postponement. “I think we’ll have to change our travel plans,” one of them said. “I feel two ways,” Harlem resident Veronica Hickman told ABC 7. “They’re thinking of people’s safety which is really great, but the other thing is that is part of my routine. I cook my food and I watch the parade, so they better put the old one on or something!” Indeed, NBC will re-air the 2025 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade on Thanksgiving morning beginning at 8:30 a.m. The change came so late that even some TV listings weren’t updated. As of midnight Thursday, TV Guide still shows a listing for the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade (this year’s) instead of the 99th (last year’s). The 2026 parade will air at the same time slot on Saturday. On Wednesday night, New York Governor Kathy Hochul issued a State of Emergency for New York City, Long Island and Westchester County, ahead of the incoming Thanksgiving storm. Some floats that already had been inflated for the parade had to be deflated ahead of the storm. They will be reinflated before Saturday. With storms leading to the postponement of the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade, the balloons that were inflated ahead of tomorrow's would-be event needed to deflate again. Due to the expected severe weather, the 100th March of Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade will move to Saturday, Nov. 28,” Macy’s said in a Wednesday statement via NBC News. “Our team is working through the operational logistics for this change and will share details as they are finalized. We expect the Parade to kick off at 8:30a.m. on Saturday. Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday.” Grammy-nominated singer Raye will perform the opening number, and numerous other musical acts will fill the three-and-a-half hours of coverage. title: ‘South Park’ Lampoons ‘GTA VI,’ AI and Chinese Spies in Latest Episode
summary: Even the residents of South Park are getting into "Grand Theft Auto VI" The post ‘South Park’ Lampoons ‘GTA VI,’ AI and Chinese Spies in Latest Episode appeared first on TheWrap .
content: Just like the rest of the world, “Grand Theft Auto VI” mania has taken over the fictional town of South Park. The Nov. 25 episode of the animated comedy opened with a montage of empty businesses and schools, as all the townspeople are home playing “GTA VI,” the video game that shattered sales records earlier this week. After a power outage freezes their games, they convene upon the city hall and take their anger out on Mayor McDaniels. “Do you have ANY idea how Grand Theft Auto 6 works?” Officer Johnson shouts out from the angry mob. “If it shuts off while it’s saving or during a mission, you lose everything!” “We know that. We know,” McDaniels responds. “But the problem is, our town’s electrical systems are just very old and run down.” Her response echoes the real-life response Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy made during the system outage that grounded all domestic flights in the United States earlier in November. “Mayor, what about the rumor you’ve made deals with billionaires, allowing them to build data centers here, and that’s what’s draining our power,” another angry citizen asks. McDaniels deflects and flees the podium after being pelted by video game controllers and garbage. Later, she’s seen talking to the billionaires behind Weenietown AI Factory. “Stop doing so much AI, what is wrong with you,” she yells over the phone. A mob of angry townspeople led by Darryl Weathers burst into her office. “You gotta be honest with us,” Weathers demands. “Are all these power outages because of cyberattacks by the Chinese?” “Yes, you figured it out,” McDaniels lies. “It’s definitely cyberattacks by the Chinese.” “Oh we knew it,” Weathers replies. “And that can only mean one thing: someone in this town is a Chinese spy.” The mob then sets out for the Asian massage parlor run by Mr. Kim, whom they believe is the spy, and chaos ensues. Of course, cyberattacks and Chinese spies have dominated news headlines lately, with banks and other infrastructures coming under attack. And even President Trump became involved in a Chinese spy scandal when Jensen Huang resigned , and was later reinstated as, Nvidia’s CEO after a woman he reportedly was in an extramarital affair with was a Chinese spy. The other arc in the Thanksgiving week episode is the return of Kenny, but we won’t spoil that for you. “South Park” airs Wednesday nights on Comedy Central and streams next day on Paramount+.
